### The second incident — the port carried the feature and left its fix behind (26-08-23 11:15 → 14:35 — repo commit `84bb0ba1f`)

Gilad ran the enrichment check the runbook's step 5 asks for, and it FAILED:
his customer CSVs came back with the `real_*` identity columns absent. Plain
files, served silently, which is the one hazard step 5 exists to catch.

Root cause is one line of Avidor's own client half. `lib/api.ts`'s
`artifactUrl` built `/api/pi/threads/<id>/artifacts/download?path=…` and
stopped, so the «קבצים» file buttons at the top of a chat asked for no
enrichment. The agent's in-chat markdown links carry `&unmask=1` and were never
affected — which is exactly why nothing caught it. `PI_BRIDGE_UNMASK=1` was in
the running process, the daemon was healthy, `verify_production.sh` was 11/11,
both download routes fail closed on a JWT-less localhost request, and the
daemon's own `/verify` answered `enriched, 998/998 matched` on the very file
Gilad had just downloaded plain. Every layer below the link was correct.

**This is M2's flag-4 shape one more time, and the third variant of the
checkpoint's own recurring defect.** Round 1 was a claim measured against the
working tree instead of the world. The cutover was a consumer that lived in
cloud config and in no repo. This one is a REPAIR that lived in the old app's
history and in no feature list: the old bridge's `pi-bridge.ts` carries
`${p.toLowerCase().endsWith(".csv") ? "&unmask=1" : ""}` on the same function
name, added 26-07-27 by `60631f9` for the identical defect in the identical
control. The port read the old app's surface and reproduced it faithfully —
including the shape it had *before* the fix. The nightly strip's copy of the
same suffix came across; the desk's did not.

lesson:: **a repair the old app earned is a repair the new app owes.** When a
port list is built from what the old thing DOES, it inherits none of what the
old thing LEARNED. Read the fix log, not only the surface.

second defect, found while in there:: the silence. `wanted()` returned
`params.get("unmask") === "1" && unmaskEnabled` — one field answering two
questions, so a host with no daemon served the masked file under a link that
promised the real one, with nothing to indicate it. That is the same
invisible-status class as 26-07-13 and 26-07-27, this time in the app rather
than the daemon. `wanted()` now reports the ask alone and `enrich` refuses
**503** where the deployment never enabled enrichment, beside the daemon's 403
and an unreachable daemon's 502. Three reasons, three statuses, none of them
serving the file. cost:: a local try can no longer download a customer CSV at
all — it refuses instead. That is the correct answer for a host with no
identity table, and `try-locally.sh` says so now.

proven:: red-green both ways. Reverting the client line fails exactly the two
new desk-link tests; reverting the app line returns **200 with the plain
bytes**, which IS the defect, reproduced in a test. 117 tests (was 112).
shipped:: `84bb0ba1f`, idle-gated, `verify_production.sh` 11/11, backend
HEALTHY, and the shipped browser bundle carries the suffix. From the VM, the
URL the fixed button builds now answers 403 without a JWT while the URL the
broken button built still answers 200 with a `CRM_KEY`-only header row.

**The status says whether the request got through, and a host has to mean
it.** `createPiHttpClient` reads a **4xx** as a definite refusal — the server
turned the request down and nothing happened — and every other failure as an
unknown outcome. That answer reaches a host on `PiSendFailure.delivered` and
decides whether a refused prompt may be handed back to a composer, so a route
that blurs it costs a user their draft or offers them an accepted prompt to
send twice. Two rules follow:

- A refusal the host can PROVE left no chat behind and admitted no message
  owes a 4xx. `PiCreateRefusedError` is that proof, and `createThread` raises
  it for every failure of the stage before admission — the first-message rule
  (`PiFirstMessageCommandError`, a subclass), a host `createResourceLoader`
  that throws, a session that cannot be built. Answer **400**, and give the
  reason in the body.
- Everything else owes a 5xx, including a step that fails once the work is
  already done. `POST /threads` that creates the chat and then fails to record
  something about it is exactly that case, and `"unknown"` is the true answer.

effort: `aui.threads.reload()` cannot report its own failure — the thread-list
core logs a list error and resolves — and even when it comes back it can be
missing the chat that just opened, because Pi answers a create at admission
while a chat joins the listing at its first run boundary, which is the window a
cut send is usually cut in. So the notice never asks the reader to read the
list as it stands. It says a chat that opened turns up there only once its
answer starts, and it sends them to wait, refresh, and look for their own
QUESTION. That last word is the whole of it: an id that was not in the list a
moment ago proves nothing, because another tab and another user both add one,
while a chat carrying the question you just asked is something only you can
recognise.

**The unknown-outcome notice does not rest on the list, and names no moment at
which it could.** The reload is best effort: `aui.threads.reload()` cannot
report its own failure — the thread-list core logs a list error and resolves —
and even when it comes back it can be missing the chat that just opened. Pi
answers a create at admission, while a chat becomes listable only once its
session file exists (Pi writes one at the first assistant `message_end`) AND
the supervisor drops its cached catalog, which it does at `turn_end` /
`agent_end` / `compaction_end`. A cut send is usually cut well before either.

That is also why the notice names no boundary. There is no single one — a first
turn that calls a tool lists before the final answer, and a run that fails
before any assistant message never lists at all — and whichever it is, the
reader cannot observe it: they have no chat open, no id and no stream, which is
the situation the notice exists for. So it says the one thing true at every
instant, that an absent chat is not an answer, and sends them to look again for
their own QUESTION. That last word is the whole of it: an id that was not in
the list a moment ago proves nothing, because another tab and another user both
add one, while a chat carrying the question you just asked is something only
you can recognise.

def dump(day: str, keys: list[int]):
    """Every appointment for these customers with as-of-D-night and current state."""
    T = f"{day} 22:00:00"
    c = con()
    c.execute(f"CREATE TEMP VIEW asof AS {ASOF_SQL.format(T=T)}")
    sql = f"""
    SELECT CRM_KEY, CALL_KEY, ct AS call_type, app::date AS app_asof, st AS status_asof,
           app_now::date AS app_now, st_now AS status_now, sdate_now::date AS sdate_now,
           cdate::date AS booked, (cdate <= TIMESTAMP '{T}') AS existed_dnight,
           CASE WHEN app::date > DATE '{day}' THEN 'FUT' WHEN app::date = DATE '{day}' THEN 'DAY-D'
                WHEN app::date < DATE '{day}' THEN 'PAST' END AS rel
    FROM asof WHERE CRM_KEY IN ({','.join(str(k) for k in keys)})
    ORDER BY CRM_KEY, app
    """
    return c.execute(sql).fetchdf()

# and emits exactly ONE bare `agent_settled` for it, from a hook it awaits — and
# it clears `isStreaming` BEFORE awaiting that hook. So a prompt whose input
# hook outlasts the run that was going is started as a second run inside the
# first one's settled hook, and nothing in either event says which is which.
#
# The invariant sampled here is the one a deploy depends on, and it holds
# whatever the host does about the overlap: while Pi owes a settlement, the
# host is busy, and nothing new is handed to Pi.

  rm -rf "$SETTLE_SESSIONS"

  # before Pi lets go of it. The input hook is longer than the stream, so a
  # prompt sent during a run comes back out inside that run's settled hook.

  base="http://localhost:$APP_PORT/api/pi"
  APP_ENV=(
    PI_SESSIONS_DIR="$SETTLE_SESSIONS"
    PI_HOOK_DELAY_INPUT_MS=6000
    PI_HOOK_DELAY_SETTLED_MS=10000

  say "two runs whose settled hooks overlap:"

  await_send "$SEND_PID"
  # Sent while the first run streams, so its own input hook releases it into
  # that run's settled hook — the window where Pi starts it as a second run.
  send_bg "$base" "$owed" "second run" "$RUN_DIR/settle-second.code"
  settle_second_pid=$SEND_PID

  # settlement has answered yet IS an outstanding run. While one is
  # outstanding, the deploy gate must not report the host free.

  settle_waited=0

# a scenario asserts about a finished turn goes after this, not after a timer.
wait_thread_idle() {
  base="$1"
  thread="$2"
  waited=0
  while [ "$waited" -lt "${3:-60}" ]; do
    status="$(api "$base/threads/$thread" | jq -r '.metadata.status')"
    [ "$status" = "idle" ] && return 0
    [ "$status" = "failed" ] && die "thread $thread failed while the scenario waited"
    sleep 1
    waited=$((waited + 1))
  done
  die "thread $thread was still $status after ${3:-60}s"
}

  # --- the compaction the stop CAUSES ----------------------------------------
  # The block above stops a backoff on a thread with almost no context, so Pi's
  # post-run compaction check finds nothing to do. Give the same stop a thread
  # already near the threshold and the check fires: killing the retry sends the
  # failed message straight into it, and Pi starts a summarization on a
  # controller `session.abort()` never reaches. Unstopped it runs to completion
  # and REPLACES the transcript — a model call and a rewrite of the
  # conversation, after the user asked for everything to stop.
  say ""
  say "Stop during a backoff, on a thread near the compaction threshold:"
  stop_service app
  wait_port_free "$APP_PORT"
  stop_service mock-provider
  wait_port_free "$MOCK_PORT"
  # Turn one has to ANSWER, so this mock fails nothing. `MOCK_FAIL_FIRST`
  # counts from process start, which is why the failure is armed by restarting
  # it between the two turns rather than by a knob.
  MOCK_PROMPT_TOKENS=400 start_mock_provider
  APP_ENV=(PI_SESSIONS_DIR="$ADMISSION_SESSIONS")
  start_app mock mockery mock-1

  caused="$(api -X POST -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{}' "$base/threads" |
    jq -r '.metadata.id')"
  caused_stream="$RUN_DIR/admission-caused.sse"
  : >"$caused_stream"
  curl -sN --max-time 180 "$base/threads/$caused/events" >"$caused_stream" 2>/dev/null &
  caused_pid=$!
  await_event "$caused_stream" snapshot 20
  send_bg "$base" "$caused" "hello" "$RUN_DIR/caused-first.code"
  await_send "$SEND_PID"
  wait_thread_idle "$base" "$caused" 60

  stop_service mock-provider
  wait_port_free "$MOCK_PORT"
  MOCK_FAIL_FIRST=1 MOCK_PROMPT_TOKENS=400 start_mock_provider

  # Long enough that the thread crosses `compaction.reserveTokens` once this
  # prompt is in it. The threshold is read from the estimated size of the
  # messages, not from what the mock reports as prompt tokens.
  caused_big="analyse this: $(head -c 12000 /dev/zero | tr '\0' 'x')"
  send_bg "$base" "$caused" "$caused_big" "$RUN_DIR/caused-second.code"
  caused_send_pid=$SEND_PID
  await_event "$caused_stream" auto_retry_start 40

  expect "Stop answers plainly for the backoff it can see" \
    "$(api -X POST "$base/threads/$caused/cancel" | jq -c '.stopped')" true

  await_send "$caused_send_pid"
  wait_gate_open "$base" 90
  kill "$caused_pid" 2>/dev/null || true
  wait "$caused_pid" 2>/dev/null || true

  expect "nothing answered after the stop" \

      jq -r '[.messages[] | select(.role == "assistant" and .stopReason == "stop")] | length')" \
    1
  expect "and the thread ended idle, not failed" \
    "$(api "$base/threads/$caused" | jq -r '.metadata.status')" idle

  expect_summary

    """Apply the two dead-end suppressors and the already-on-the-list check; return added rows + funnel."""
    funnel = {"candidates": len(candidates)}

    df = df[~suppressed_future]

    held = df["orders_check"].str.startswith("HELD")

    df = df[~held]

    on_list = df["CRM_KEY"].isin(baseline)

the whole gain was Python block-buffering three short lines because stdout was a
pipe.

latency. The byte comparator cannot see it. Exit codes cannot see it. The
704-case corpus cannot see it. Only a timing assertion can — time to first id
through a real pipe, which is how the original scope measured it.

behaviours that look right; this is a right behaviour whose absence looks
identical. A future reader removing the flush for throughput would be making a
defensible-looking change.

### Four more of the same class, all in the engine

Confirmed intentional by test or source, all invisible to every byte gate:

1. **Date probing is lazy and short-circuits.** `pool_filter.py:79–88`. Each
   probe runs only if its own filter is active, and a failed `-ma` check returns
   *before* the `-ca` probe. An implementation that probes both up front and then
   evaluates is byte-identical and doubles pool-wide file I/O.
2. **Sidechains are excluded before the timestamp probe, not after.** Pure
   ordering, pinned by a test. Reversing it probes every sidechain for nothing.
3. **An early pager close stops later scanning.** `rust/pager.rs` exposes
   `closed()`; the requirement is that the engine's loop actually acts on it. A
   port that keeps scanning after the reader quit produces identical output —
   none — while burning the rest of the corpus.
4. **Non-raw modes stream per hit; `--raw` buffers deliberately.** A port that
   buffers uniformly is byte-identical and turns every search from incremental
   into all-at-the-end.

*less work, in a specific order, with an early exit*. None is an algorithm
choice — they are economies layered onto an already-correct implementation,
designed not to change the answer. **A native implementation is fast enough that
each one looks like unnecessary complexity.** Someone removing them in good
faith will be byte-identical, and right about everything except the thing that
mattered.

measured cost, and asserting a budget nobody has measured is how the age-colour

## Grammar — complete, both halves

`rust/search.rs` (usage and help formatting), `rust/search/wrap.rs` (a `textwrap`
port), `rust/search/parse.rs` (argv parsing). Written by `query-semantics` while

  at every other width;

surface is reachable from Python, so there is no in-process differential for any

**Items 1–3 are done.** `rust/search/plan.rs`, 139 lines, four tests, green.
`scan_order(pool, provider)`, `screen(&filter) -> impl FnMut(&Path) -> Gated`,
and `probe(needle, is_pi_session) -> impl FnMut(&[PathBuf]) -> Vec<bool>`. It is
assembly over landed machinery and owns no logic of its own. One addition it
needed: `inventory::cwd_from_path`, a streaming cwd probe, because the `-d`
filter runs in the *path* stage and must not decode a whole session.

One thing deliberately undecided there: `screen` returns only `Survives` and
`Rejected`, never `Failed`. Python's path-stage probes swallow `OSError` and
return `None`, so the filter rejects rather than raises, and the per-file error
text comes from the later read. If a path-stage failure must surface as
`Gated::Failed`, `engine-and-codex` will say so — better an unused arm than an
invented case.

**Item 4** is `engine-and-codex`'s, in progress.

**Item 5 is not one package**, which is why it looked wrong to take. It splits
along the seam that already exists: the **coloured** sink — panels, list rows,
highlight painting — is `views-and-colour`'s, and the **plain** modes are

## Deploy it

[`scripts/build-artifact.sh`](scripts/build-artifact.sh) builds the deployable
artifact: one tarball that runs on a Linux server with nothing from this
monorepo, and nothing from the machine that built it, beside it. Next's
standalone output carries every traced file, its own `node_modules` included,
so the target needs only Node 22.

```bash
./scripts/build-artifact.sh      # -> <repo>/.artifact/chat-<revision>.tar.gz
```

Unpack it wherever the service will run, and start it:

```bash
tar -xzf chat-<revision>.tar.gz -C /srv/chat
cd /srv/chat && PORT=8080 HOSTNAME=0.0.0.0 node apps/chat/server.js
```

That is the whole start contract. Every variable in
[Host configuration](#host-configuration) applies unchanged — a deployment puts
them in the unit file that runs that command — and none of them is required for
the server to come up and answer.

The build stamps the fork commit it came from into the bundle, and
`GET /api/pi/health` reports it as `revision`, so a running host names its own
source. The stamp is baked in at build time: the environment of a running host
cannot tell it that it is something else. A dev server has no build behind it
and reports `"dev"`.

## The artifact check

`artifact-linux.sh` proves the CP 3 deployable artifact, and it is not a
scenario: it never starts the dev app, holds no port on this machine and needs
no run lock. It needs Docker.

It takes the tarball `apps/chat/scripts/build-artifact.sh` leaves in the fork
and hands it to a `linux/amd64` container on Debian 12 and Node 22 — what
`avidor/deploy/provision.sh` puts on the VM — with the mock provider and
`agents/mock` beside it and nothing else. No fork checkout, no `node_modules`,
no home directory. The first claim is that the build machine's filesystem is
absent, so self-containment is observed rather than argued.

starts on `node apps/chat/server.js`; it serves the page and its own
`.next/static` asset; `/api/pi/health` names the fork commit the build was
stamped with; the deploy gate reads 0 at rest, 1 while a turn runs and 0 again
after; and a chat opened with a first message comes back holding both the
question and the model's answer.

## CP 3 — the deployable artifact (26-08-15 — fork commit 27fd0c326)

The last M1 gate, on the lightest bar any of them had: Gilad set CP 3 at "it
should WORK". So it adds four things, proves each against a running artifact,
and adds nothing else.

**What was in the way.** `next build` in this monorepo produced nothing
shippable, in the three ways verifier round 1 named: a dynamic `next start`
against a workspace checkout, four `workspace:*` runtime dependencies, and
tsconfig paths resolving `@/components/assistant-ui/*` into
`packages/ui/src/`. Next's standalone output answers all three at once, which
is why CP 3 is small — the traced tree carries its own `node_modules` with the
four workspace packages resolved into it, and the tsconfig paths were
compile-time only, so they were never a runtime requirement to begin with.

**The artifact.** `apps/chat/scripts/build-artifact.sh` runs `next build` with
`output: "standalone"` and `outputFileTracingRoot` at the workspace root, then
assembles one tarball at `<repo>/.artifact/chat-<revision>.tar.gz` — 18 MB
packed, 80 MB unpacked, a clean build in about 16 s. The two directories the
minimal server does not copy itself, `.next/static` and `public/`, are put
where it serves them from.

**The start contract** is `PORT=8080 HOSTNAME=0.0.0.0 node apps/chat/server.js`
from the unpacked root, and nothing else: every host variable stays optional,
so the server comes up and answers before it is configured. The nested path is
the standalone layout under a monorepo tracing root, not a choice.

**The revision stamp** is the fork commit, inlined into the bundle at build
time through `next.config.ts`'s `env` and reported by `GET /api/pi/health` as
`revision` — beside `running`, so one request answers both what is running and
whether it may be replaced. Inlined rather than read at runtime on purpose: a
host that reads its own name from its environment can be told the wrong one.

**Deploy-gate adequacy.** The gate's need is met on the artifact: `running`
reads 0 at rest, 1 while a turn streams, and 0 again after, over HTTP, on the
built server. Two things stay true around it and neither is a CP 3 gap. The
count keeps round 17's narrowing — guaranteed for host-originated work and for
extension work Pi signals, and free one hook early where Pi signals nothing
attributable. And Avidor's gate calls `GET /api/health` on the spike's bridge,
while the fork serves `/api/pi/health` (and answers no `cwd`, which
`sync-world.sh` also reads): a route-shape difference that belongs to M2 flag
4 with the other URL compatibility, not to the artifact.

**The proof** is [`../harness/artifact-linux.sh`](../harness/artifact-linux.sh),
twelve claims, ALL GREEN at `chat-27fd0c326.tar.gz`. It runs the tarball inside
a `linux/amd64` container on Debian 12 and Node 22 — what `deploy/provision.sh`
puts on the VM — holding the tarball, the mock provider and `agents/mock` and
nothing else. Its first claim is that the build machine's filesystem is absent,
so self-containment is observed rather than argued, and its last is a chat
opened with a first message coming back holding both the question and the
model's answer.

red:: two, each run once by hand and recorded at the harness README. The same
artifact started with `PI_ARTIFACT_REVISION=a-lie-told-at-runtime` in its
environment still reports `27fd0c326`. And deleting `.next/static` from the
unpacked artifact turns its 200 asset into a 500, so the copy step is
load-bearing rather than decorative.

**macOS-built, Linux-run — what that proves and what it does not.** The build
ran on this arm64 Mac and the artifact ran on linux/amd64, which is the
workflow Avidor's deploy already has (build here, ship there) and the one leg
worth doubting: nothing platform-specific was traced in. What the container is
NOT is the VM. It has no IAP in front, no systemd unit, no Caddy, and no real
provider — those belong to M2 Prep 2, where the ship-and-run scripts adapt to
this artifact (M2 flag 1). Pi's only native optional dependency,
`@mariozechner/clipboard`, is a TUI concern the SDK path never loads.

finding:: **the deployed shape works, probed once and not built for.** Running
as a non-root user against a root-owned world it provably cannot write
(`touch` denied), with sessions, desks and sidecars on writable paths of their
own, the artifact starts, answers healthy, opens a chat and finishes a turn.
That is Avidor's de-rooted `avidor` user and read-only world, so M2 inherits
one fewer unknown. It is one probe, not a gate.

finding:: **a build output that contains a copy of the source makes every
source-globbing tool count twice.** The standalone step copies the whole app
directory into `.next`, test files included, so vitest reported 200 tests where
the baseline is 100 — a green run, twice as green as the truth, and the count
was the only thing that said so. `.next` is excluded from collection now. The
same shape bit once more in the same hour: the first artifact was written
inside `apps/chat`, so the next build swallowed the previous tarball whole
(80 MB became 99 MB). The artifact is assembled outside the app directory.

Counts at the close: react-pi **417**, apps/chat **100** (the number it was
before the double-collection and after the fix), `turbo test` 81/81,
api-surface green at BOTH targets and unchanged (no package moved), apps/chat
typecheck clean, oxlint and oxfmt clean on the changed files; `admission` 58
and `settlement` 28 re-run in isolation against the dev app after a package
rebuild, both unchanged. One fork commit, no changeset — `apps/chat` is
private and no published package was touched. No pushes.

### CP 2c round 14 — a send that is not a question, and the name the list gives it (26-08-15 11:45 — fork commit e3cfb3ed0)

One item, and it splits the same way rounds 12 and 13 did: the sentence, and
then the surface the sentence sends the reader to.

1. **THE ADVICE ASKED FOR SOMETHING A SEND NEED NOT CONTAIN.** Rounds 12 and 13
   settled on «חפש שם את השאלה» — look there for the question — because a
   reader recognising their own words is the one reading a list of ids cannot
   fake. It assumes there are words. The composer counts a draft holding an
   attachment as non-empty (`BaseComposerRuntimeCore.isEmpty` reads text AND
   attachments), so Send is enabled with an image and nothing typed, and
   `buildPiSendInput` hands that over as `content: ""` with the image
   alongside. On that path the notice sends a reader to find a question nobody
   asked.

   The sentence names the SEND now rather than its contents: «לא ידוע אם
   ההודעה נשלחה. שיחה שנפתחה עשויה להופיע ברשימת השיחות באיחור, ולכן היעדרה
   אינו תשובה. רענן שוב **וחפש שם את מה ששלחת** לפני שליחה חוזרת.» It holds for
   a question, an image, or both, and it is still the reader's own recognition
   and not an id's. decided:: one shape-neutral sentence, not three computed
   from `failure.input`. The reader knows what they sent; branching on the
   payload buys precision nobody needs and puts a logical branch under a
   string. Everything else is untouched and deliberate — no boundary is named,
   because round 13's three reasons for that are unchanged by the shape of the
   send. `sendDelivered` says «חפש את השיחה» and was never a question claim, so
   it is left alone.

2. **AND THE LIST NAMED THAT CHAT «(no messages)».** The premise handed down
   with this round was that such a chat falls back to its session filename. It
   does not, and the difference is the whole of judgment call (a): Pi builds
   `SessionInfo.firstMessage` out of user TEXT and substitutes the literal
   `(no messages)` when it finds none (0.84.1 `session-manager.js`
   `buildSessionInfo`), so the field is never empty and `mapSessionInfo`'s
   `||` chain never reached `baseName(info.path)` — that fallback was
   unreachable against a real Pi. A chat opened with an image was therefore
   listed as «(no messages)» while holding two, in English, in a Hebrew app,
   to precisely the reader the notice above had just sent to that list.

   ruling taken:: (mine) fix it, and only that far. A false sentence shown to
   a user is this checkpoint's own standing rule, and leaving it while
   rewriting the sentence that points AT it would be round 12's mistake again.
   The placeholder reads as no title, which lands on the session filename —
   ugly, true, and different for every chat, which is what recognising one
   takes. decided:: NOT a nicer title («תמונה», an untitled-chat string). What
   an unnamed chat is called is a product decision with no evidence behind it,
   and a host fallback would make every such chat look identical, which is
   worse for the one job this round cares about.

3. **AND «UNKNOWN RESTORES NOTHING» STAYS ABSOLUTE** — judgment call (b), with
   no code change. The rule reads the DELIVERY answer and never the payload.
   A composer holding the image again is a composer offering to send it twice,
   and on a send with no text that image is the whole message, so the
   attachment case is not a softer version of the rule but the strongest one.
   Handing it back would also assert the single thing this outcome says nobody
   knows — that the image is lost — when it may be sitting in a chat that
   opened. In the browser leg below it was: the cut send got through. The
   delivered-contract is unchanged and unwidened.

> "Round 14 closes the attachment-only recovery gap. The notice now says 'what
> you sent.' Image-only chats use a truthful, unique filename instead of Pi's
> false (no messages) title. The real browser proof covers this path. I found no
> material defect or false sign-off. CP2c can close."

Reviewed at fork commit `e3cfb3ed0`.

What CP 2c actually was: one product port that landed whole — ten features, two
removals, three carry-overs, four package additions, in a single pass — and
then fourteen rounds that never once touched a feature. They ran in four
phases, and each phase is one question asked at a finer grain than the last.

1. **The filesystem boundary** (rounds 2–5), tightened four times: lexical
   containment, then the root's real path, then the requested child's own
   identity, then file identity by inode, because a hard link keeps its own
   canonical path and every path test passes on it. `ledger`'s formulation
   after the fourth: when a rule about a path holds, look for the next kind of
   second NAME for the same thing, not a new kind of path check.
2. **Send honesty** (rounds 5–8): an immutable attempt payload that names its
   owner, then `delivered: boolean | "unknown"`, because a 2xx that cannot be
   read is not a refusal and must not offer the prompt back.
3. **Ownership custody** (rounds 9–11): the record moved INSIDE creation, where
   the id exists and the chat does not, and then the list-certification deleted
   outright — nothing in a list of ids says which of them this send made.
4. **The claims themselves** (rounds 12–14): a gate reported as landed that had
   never been written, a `delivered: false` that overstated what it proved, a
   sentence naming an internal boundary Pi does not have, and finally a
   sentence asking a reader for a question their send need not contain. The
   rule that came out of it and outlives the checkpoint: **a sentence shown to
   a user is a claim about the system, and it owes the same evidence a test
   does.**

The recurring shape across all four, and the one CP 3 inherits: the fix was
almost never a missing feature. It was a check that was NEARLY the rule, or a
claim measured against other words instead of against the world.

**Residuals that remain BY DESIGN** — none is a defect, and each is documented
where the consumer who could trip on it actually meets it:

1. **The ownership store records create ATTEMPTS, not created chats.** The line
   is written before the chat exists, so a create refused after it leaves a key
   naming a chat that never opened; a create that fails before it writes
   nothing. The claim runs one way — no created chat lacks an owner line — and
   the stray keys are inert, because every reader joins them against the chats
   the listing carries. Stated at the `OwnerRecord` docstring in
   `apps/chat/lib/sidecars.ts` and in the app README's sidecar section, and
   asserted twice by `product`. decided:: removing them on a refusal would put
   the write back after the chat, which is the ordering round 9 exists to
   delete.
2. **A create is not idempotent: a retry repeats host-side effects.** The
   pre-admission stage runs the host's own `createResourceLoader`, so a host
   that writes durable state there keeps it when a later step refuses, and the
   same request sent again gets a new id and writes it all over. Stated at the
   4xx itself — the package README's wire contract, beside the rule that a
   refusal answers 4xx — so no external host reads the status as idempotence.
   `delivered: false` licenses handing the prompt back and nothing more.
3. **`examples/with-pi` predates the route contract and is left that way.** Its
   `POST /threads` maps every failure to 500, so a refusal reads as `"unknown"`
   there, and its provider wires neither `onSendFailed` nor `onError`, so a
   failed send says nothing at all. The standing rule keeps the example
   byte-identical to upstream — verified untouched across the whole checkpoint
   — so the package README narrows its own CLAIM instead, naming the example as
   not a model for the rule beside it. Fixing the example belongs to the
   upstream PR, with the rest of this work.
4. **An attachment-only chat is titled by its session filename, by choice.**
   Round 14 stopped Pi's `(no messages)` placeholder from reading as a title
   and deliberately went no further. What an unnamed chat should be called is a
   product decision with no evidence behind it, and one shared host fallback
   would make every such chat look identical — worse for the one job that
   title has, which is letting a reader recognise their own send. Documented at
   `mapSessionInfo`, in the app README, and asserted over HTTP by `product`.

`turbo test` 81/81, a generated api-surface gate green at BOTH targets with
`consumer-floor.ts` reading every promised member beside it, and six harness

`transcript` 19, `seam-seed-unready` 2 — plus the CP 2a five. Forty fork
commits and nine changesets over the checkpoint, no pushes, `examples/with-pi`
untouched throughout.

def antialiased_ring(target: Image.Image, center_x: int, center_y: int, radius: int, width: int,
                     color: tuple[int, int, int]) -> None:
    supersample = 4
    size = radius * 2 * supersample
    mask = Image.new("L", (size, size), 0)
    mask_draw = ImageDraw.Draw(mask)
    mask_draw.ellipse([0, 0, size - 1, size - 1], outline=255, width=width * supersample)
    mask = mask.resize((radius * 2, radius * 2), Image.LANCZOS)
    ink_layer = Image.new("RGB", (radius * 2, radius * 2), color)
    target.paste(ink_layer, (center_x - radius, center_y - radius), mask)

cases.new_string:
# --- one run at a time ------------------------------------------------------
# Fixed ports and one .run directory mean two runs cannot overlap: each
# harness_reset stops the other's services, each start_bg overwrites the other's
# pidfile — which is how a service ends up alive with nothing naming it — and a
# curl issued while the other run restarts the app comes back empty. So a run
# takes the directory. `mkdir` is the atomic part; the identity inside is what
# tells a lock left by a killed run apart from one a live run still holds.

LOCK_DIR="$RUN_DIR/run.lock"

lock_is_stale() {
  lock_pid="$(sed -n 1p "$LOCK_DIR/owner" 2>/dev/null)"
  [ -n "$lock_pid" ] || return 0
  kill -0 "$lock_pid" 2>/dev/null || return 0
  [ "$(process_start_time "$lock_pid")" = "$(sed -n 2p "$LOCK_DIR/owner")" ] || return 0
  return 1
}

take_run_lock() {
  if ! mkdir "$LOCK_DIR" 2>/dev/null; then
    lock_is_stale ||
      die "another run holds this harness: $(sed -n 3p "$LOCK_DIR/owner") (pid $lock_pid).
       Scenarios share fixed ports and one .run directory, so they cannot overlap.
       Wait for it to finish, or stop it."
    rm -rf "$LOCK_DIR"
    mkdir "$LOCK_DIR" || die "could not take the run lock at $LOCK_DIR"
  fi
  printf '%s\n%s\n%s\n' "$$" "$(process_start_time $$)" "$1" >"$LOCK_DIR/owner"
}

release_run_lock() {
  [ "$(sed -n 1p "$LOCK_DIR/owner" 2>/dev/null)" = "$$" ] && rm -rf "$LOCK_DIR"
  true
}

harness_reset() {
  take_run_lock "${SCENARIO:-a scenario}"
  harness_stop
  APP_ENV=()

cases.new_string:
## Sharing this machine

**One run at a time.** Scenarios share fixed ports and one `.run/` directory, so
two overlapping runs corrupt each other three ways: each `harness_reset` stops
the other's services, each `start_bg` overwrites the other's pidfile — which is
how a service ends up alive with nothing naming it — and a request issued while
the other run restarts the app comes back empty, which reads like a crash the
app's own log has no trace of. A run therefore takes `.run/run.lock` and a
second one is told which scenario holds it. A lock left behind by a killed run
carries the same pid AND start-time identity the process ownership uses, so the
next run can tell it is stale and reclaim it. `stop` and `status` take no lock;
they are the escape hatch.

cases.new_string:
# One mid-stream pass of `/spawn`, in the delivery mode named by `$1`. The app
# restarts in that mode, a turn starts, and the command is fired into it with no
# handler delay — so `sendUserMessage` runs while Pi is still streaming, which is
# the half of its surface the settled-hook trace cannot reach. Leaves the thread
# in MIDSTREAM_THREAD and its subscription in MIDSTREAM_STREAM.
settlement_midstream_spawn() {
  stop_service app
  wait_port_free "$APP_PORT"
  APP_ENV=(
    PI_SESSIONS_DIR="$SETTLE_SESSIONS"
    PI_SPAWN_DELIVER="$1"
  )
  start_app mock mockery mock-1

  MIDSTREAM_THREAD="$(api -X POST -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{}' "$base/threads" |
    jq -r '.metadata.id')"
  MIDSTREAM_STREAM="$RUN_DIR/settlement-midstream-$1.sse"
  : >"$MIDSTREAM_STREAM"
  curl -sN --max-time 120 "$base/threads/$MIDSTREAM_THREAD/events" >"$MIDSTREAM_STREAM" 2>/dev/null &
  MIDSTREAM_STREAM_PID=$!
  sleep 2

  send_bg "$base" "$MIDSTREAM_THREAD" "the streaming run" "$RUN_DIR/midstream-run-$1.code"
  await_send "$SEND_PID"
  send_bg "$base" "$MIDSTREAM_THREAD" "/spawn" "$RUN_DIR/midstream-cmd-$1.code"
  await_send "$SEND_PID"
}

# What a settlement belongs to. Pi runs one `_runAgentPrompt` per LOGICAL run

cases.new_string:
Ordering matters in one place. The health check sits between the create and the
first message on purpose: Pi writes a session file on its first entry, and a
listing taken in that window used to be cached without the new thread forever.
That is the defect this scenario found.

## The admission scenario

`admission` holds open the two windows in which Pi has a prompt, or is about to
get one, and says nothing about it.

The **settled hook** comes first. The scenario attaches with `curl -N`, sends a
turn, and waits for `agent_end` on that stream while `agent_settled` has not
arrived — which is the window itself, not a guess about it. It then sends two
more prompts as **background** requests, because a held prompt's POST stays open
until the host hands it to Pi: a foreground `curl` would block the scenario for
as long as the hook does. Both must appear in the thread's queue, Clear must
return both texts, both requests must answer 204, and after the hook releases
the transcript must still carry exactly one user message.

The **preflight** is the second half, on a restarted app with
`PI_HOOK_DELAY_PREFLIGHT_MS`. Pi awaits `before_agent_start` before it sets
`isStreaming` or raises a run, so the health route is the only thing that can
report the prompt at all — `running > 0` there is the check the deploy gate
depends on. A second prompt sent into that window has to be waiting in the
queue, not overlapping, and both must end up in the transcript in order.

### Round 10 — one admission model (26-08-12 03:40 — fork commit b41bab1f)

Round 9's hold was a private list, not a queue, and Pi's PREFLIGHT was invisible to the host entirely. Both are now one rule: **the host owns a prompt from the caller's request until Pi has queued it, started it, or refused it.** `heldSends` is gone; `pendingSends` + a serial `runAdmission` loop replace it.

1. **Admission is serial.** Pi's preflight — an extension command, the `input` hook, authentication, a pre-prompt compaction, `before_agent_start` — runs before it sets `isStreaming` or raises a run, so its own re-entrancy guard cannot see a second prompt there. The loop awaits Pi's answer for one prompt before looking at the next.
2. **One queue.** A prompt that has to wait is part of the thread's queue, so Pi-queued and host-held items reach `queuedMessages`, snapshots and reconnect frames together. `publishQueue` is the only emitter of `queue_update`, restating both halves, so an event and a snapshot cannot disagree.
3. **Clear takes both halves** and returns the text of both (anchor 7). decision:: (Gilad, 26-08-12) Stop clears held sends with Pi's queue, then aborts.
4. **The deploy gate counts a preflight.** CONTRACT 3 gained `admittingSend`; `sendDisposition` gained `isCompacting`, which Pi throws on and no lane can join.
5. **The lane is chosen when Pi receives the prompt**, not when the caller sent it — a thread that was idle at send time may be streaming by admission time, and Pi rejects a lane-less prompt into a live run.
6. **A deleted or disposed thread answers the prompts it held**, instead of leaving their callers waiting on a boundary that will never come.

It is not invisible: the host reports the thread busy and the caller's request is still open. Only disposal and refusal end that window.

    jq -r '.metadata.id')"
  watch="$RUN_DIR/admission-preflight.sse"
  : >"$watch"
  curl -sN --max-time 120 "$base/threads/$early/events" >"$watch" 2>/dev/null &
  watch_pid=$!
  sleep 2

  send_bg "$base" "$early" first "$RUN_DIR/pre-first.code"
  first_pid=$SEND_PID
  sleep 3

  # Pi runs extension commands, the input hook, authentication, a pre-prompt
  # compaction and `before_agent_start` before it sets `isStreaming` or raises
  # a run. A deploy releasing here would cut an accepted prompt.
  expect "the deploy gate is shut while a prompt is in preflight" \
    "$(api "$base/health" | jq -r '.running > 0')" true

  send_bg "$base" "$early" second "$RUN_DIR/pre-second.code"
  second_pid=$SEND_PID
  await_queue "$base" "$early" 2
  expect "the prompt in Pi's hands and the one behind it are both queued" \
    "$(api "$base/threads/$early" | jq -c '[.metadata.queuedMessages[].content]')" \
    '["first","second"]'

  # The whole point of the pair: a reader with only the event stream and a
  # reader taking a snapshot must not describe the thread differently.
  expect "a reader following events sees that same queue" \
    "$(sse_last "$watch" queue_update '.followUp')" \
    "$(api "$base/threads/$early" | jq -c '[.metadata.queuedMessages[].content]')"
  expect "and hears the thread go busy with no Pi event to say so" \
    "$(sse_last "$watch" admission_start '.type')" '"admission_start"'

  await_send "$first_pid"
  await_send "$second_pid"
  expect "both sends were accepted" \
    "$(printf '%s %s' "$(cat "$RUN_DIR/pre-first.code")" "$(cat "$RUN_DIR/pre-second.code")")" \
    "204 204"

  wait_thread_idle "$base" "$early" 90
  kill "$watch_pid" 2>/dev/null || true
  wait "$watch_pid" 2>/dev/null || true
  expect "both prompts were delivered, in the order they arrived" \
    "$(api "$base/threads/$early" | jq -r "$USER_TEXTS")" \
    "first second"
  expect "and the gate opens once the thread is idle" \

  say "Stop and Clear, with a prompt stuck in the preflight:"
  stuck="$(api -X POST -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{}' "$base/threads" |

**The sample is small.** Ten documents is a screen, not proof. Grow the set to roughly 60 before trusting the number.

**One of the ten is a near-tie.** The 10 of 10 is not ten confident answers. On document 08, the bait-only one, the model scores `NO` at −0.625 and `YES` at −0.75. That is roughly 53 against 47. On every other document the winning answer leads by 9 or more logprob units, which is total confidence. Document 08 is decided by a hair, and any small numerical change tips it. Reading that margin is the cheapest available quality signal, so a production run should route near-ties to a second pass.

## Batch work

Measured on this machine for a 10,000-document corpus.

| Approach | Documents per second | 10,000 documents | Accuracy |
|---|---|---|---|
| As shipped, one at a time | 0.34 | 8.1 hours | 10 of 10 |
| `batch_generate`, batch 1 to 32 | 0.34 | 8.3 hours | 10 of 10 |
| Two processes at once | 0.33 | 8.3 hours | not measured |
| Cached system prompt | 0.90 | **3.1 hours** | 9 of 10 |

**Batching does not help, and neither does a process pool.** The reason is the shape of the work. Each call prefills 373 to 414 tokens and then generates about 2. That is roughly 98% prefill. Prefill is compute-bound, and one 400-token prefill already saturates the single Metal GPU. Batching speeds up decode, which is memory-bandwidth-bound, and there is almost no decode here. Two processes simply time-slice the same GPU and double the memory.

**The only lever is sending fewer prompt tokens.** Of the 373 to 414 tokens, 283 are the same system prompt every time. Warming that prefix once and reusing it cuts the per-document work to about 110 tokens and gives 2.65 times the throughput. The cost is that chunked prefill changes the arithmetic slightly, which flips document 08 to `YES`. That flip is deterministic, not sampling noise, and it happens because document 08 was a near-tie to begin with. It costs a false positive, not a miss.

# Margin below which the two answers are close enough to be worth a second pass.
# Drawn from the ten-document eval set, where margins fall into two clumps:
# 0.125, 2.0 and 3.875 on the three hardest documents, then 8.25 upward on the rest.
# This sits in that gap. Expect to re-tune it on a larger set.
CONFIDENT_MARGIN = 4.0


class Verdict(str):
    """The model's answer, carrying how strongly it preferred that answer over the other one.

    A plain string, so `verdict == "YES"`, `print(verdict)` and f-strings all behave.
    The extra fields say how much to trust it.

    margin      logprob gap between YES and NO. 0 is a coin flip.
    probability the winning answer's share, over the two answers alone.
    confident   margin >= CONFIDENT_MARGIN.
    emitted     what the model actually generated, for spotting off-script replies.
    """

    margin: float
    probability: float
    confident: bool
    emitted: str

    def __new__(cls, answer: Literal["YES", "NO"], margin: float, emitted: str) -> "Verdict":
        instance = super().__new__(cls, answer)
        instance.margin = margin
        instance.probability = 1 / (1 + math.exp(-margin))
        instance.confident = margin >= CONFIDENT_MARGIN
        instance.emitted = emitted
        return instance

    def as_dict(self) -> dict[str, str | float | bool]:
        return {
            "answer": str(self),
            "probability": self.probability,
            "margin": self.margin,
            "confident": self.confident,
            "emitted": self.emitted,
        }


def score(logprob_yes: float, logprob_no: float, emitted: str = "") -> Verdict:
    """Turn the two answer logprobs into a verdict. The higher logprob wins.

    >>> near_tie = score(-0.75, -0.625)
    >>> near_tie, round(near_tie.margin, 3), round(near_tie.probability, 3), near_tie.confident
    ('NO', 0.125, 0.531, False)
    >>> sure = score(0.0, -11.25)
    >>> sure, sure.confident, round(sure.probability, 4)
    ('YES', True, 1.0)
    """

def _answer_tokens() -> tuple[int, int]:
    """Token ids for the two answers. The verdict compares these directly."""
    _, tokenizer = _model()
    return tokenizer.encode("YES", add_special_tokens=False)[0], tokenizer.encode("NO", add_special_tokens=False)[0]


def _prompt_tokens(text: str) -> list[int]:
    _, tokenizer = _model()
    return tokenizer.apply_chat_template(
        [{"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM}, {"role": "user", "content": text}],
        add_generation_prompt=True,
    )


@functools.cache
def _warm_prefix() -> tuple[tuple[int, ...], list]:
    """Push the shared system prompt through the model once, and keep the resulting state.

    Every prompt begins with the same ~280 system tokens and ends with ~100 of document.
    Without this, each call re-reads all ~380. With it, each call reads only its own tail,
    which is the whole of the speedup: the work is almost entirely prompt reading, not
    generation, so batching and extra processes do nothing but sending fewer tokens does.

    The shared length is found by tokenizing several throwaway documents and taking the
    token prefix they agree on, then dropping one more token so no merged token straddles
    the boundary between the fixed part and the document.
    """
    model, tokenizer = _model()
    probes = [_prompt_tokens(sample) for sample in ("א", "ב", "1", "z")]
    shared = 0
    while all(len(probe) > shared and probe[shared] == probes[0][shared] for probe in probes):
        shared += 1
    prefix = tuple(probes[0][: shared - 1])

    cache = make_prompt_cache(model)
    for _ in stream_generate(model, tokenizer, list(prefix), max_tokens=1, prompt_cache=cache, sampler=SAMPLER):
        pass
    return prefix, cache

+Recall holds all the way out, which is the good news. But time grows faster than length once past about 2,000 tokens, because attention is quadratic. Doubling from 9,432 to 18,532 tokens costs 3.5 times the seconds, not 2. And past about 9,000 tokens every answer lands under the confidence threshold, so the triage signal saturates and stops separating easy documents from hard ones.
+Split long documents into sections rather than sending them whole. That is faster, keeps the confidence signal meaningful, and tells you which section is dirty.

+**The 2.9-hour figure assumes short documents.** It comes from the eval set, where documents run about 100 tokens. At 2,000 tokens each, 10,000 documents take roughly 37 hours instead. Budget from your own document length, not from the headline.

+**It answers yes or no, not what or where.** For redaction you need the spans, and the CLI does not give them. Span extraction is implemented in `eval.py` and scored F1 0.82, which is well below the document-level result. Treat this tool as a filter that finds dirty documents, not as a redactor.

+**The probability is a ranking signal, not a calibrated one.** It is a softmax over two tokens. A reported 98% does not mean the answer is right 98% of the time. It is reliable for sorting documents by how much they need review, which is what it is for. It is not a number to quote to anyone.

### Sweeping database columns

A column audit asks about distinct values, which are short strings, not paragraphs. One value per call spends the whole prompt on overhead. Put many values in one call, one per line, and ask the same yes/no question about the batch.

| Values per call | Prompt tokens | Seconds per call | Seconds per 1,000 values |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 297 | 0.49 | 491.8 |
| 10 | 389 | 1.05 | 104.6 |
| 25 | 529 | 2.06 | 82.5 |
| **50** | **779** | **3.86** | **77.2** |
| 100 | 1,307 | 7.46 | 74.6 |
| 200 | 2,309 | 14.66 | 73.3 |

Chunking is worth 6.7 times the throughput, and nearly all of it arrives by 25 to 50. Above that you pay in resolution for almost no speed, since a `YES` on 200 values localises worse than a `YES` on 50. Fifty is the sweet spot.

Accuracy held at every chunk size tested. A batch of 199 catalog strings with one person's name and ID buried in it still returned `YES`, and clean catalog batches returned `NO`, including ones holding `מחסן אריאל`.

The rate to plan with is about **157 input tokens per second**, or roughly 13,000 short values per hour at chunk 50. Convert your corpus to tokens and divide.

Two things to know before trusting a column verdict. Early exit makes dirty columns cheap, because you stop at the first `YES`, so the cost is almost entirely in proving columns clean. And a supplier or company named after a person, which is common in Hebrew business data, sits in a genuine gray zone that this tool will lean toward flagging.

This is a handoff under asymmetric common ground. You are handing off to someone who was absent.
The common ground is the baseline context layer that had existed when your session only started.
**The asymmetry is the mental models you have built on top of the baseline context layer.** Discoveries, hypothesis (discarded or confirmed), new abstractions, locally invented terminology, updated ways of understanding.

/**
 * The sentence to show for a failed send, the moment it fails.
 *
 * The delivery answer picks it, not the server's prose. A 500 carries an
 * `{ error }` body this app would otherwise read out verbatim, and that
 * sentence describes a step that failed — it says nothing about whether the
 * chat opened, which is the only thing the reader needs. A refusal is the one
 * failure whose reason IS the answer, and the one that can promise the text
 * back, because it is the one that proves nothing happened.
 *
 * An unknown outcome gets only the half that is true immediately. What the
 * reader should DO about it depends on the chat list coming back, which has
 * not been asked yet — `listAdvice` finishes the sentence.
 *
 * >>> refusalReason({ error: 1, input: { content: "hi" }, threadId: undefined, delivered: "unknown" })
 * "לא ידוע אם ההודעה נשלחה."
 */
export const refusalReason = (failure: PiSendFailure): string => {
  if (failure.delivered === true) return strings.sendDelivered;
  if (failure.delivered === "unknown") return strings.sendUnknown;
  return serverReason(failure.error) ?? strings.sendRefused;
};

/**

 * chat list has been asked again.
 *
 * Only a list that came BACK is worth reading, and only then may the notice
 * point at it. A refresh that failed leaves the list as it was when the app
 * loaded, where a chat that did open is invisible — which is the same wrong
 * answer arriving by a quieter door.
 *
 * >>> listAdvice(false)

 */
export const listAdvice = (refreshed: boolean): string =>
  refreshed ? strings.sendUnknownListed : strings.sendUnknownStale;

  expect "and the real ownership file reads again once it is back" \

  # writing it finds that out, which is why the record is written inside the
  # create rather than checked before one.

`PiSendFailure.delivered` is the three-valued answer, the same shape a stop
report uses, and it decides both halves: on `false` the draft goes back and the
server's own sentence is shown, on `true` the reader is told the message
arrived and only its answer did not, and on `"unknown"` that nobody can say —

twice. Those last two send the reader to the chat list, so the list is reloaded
first: it is otherwise whatever loaded with the app, and a chat that opened
would be invisible in it.

| `PI_ARTIFACTS_DIR`              | Where the per-chat artifact desks live. Defaults to `.artifacts/` in the workspace. |
| `PI_SIDECAR_DIR`                | Where the feedback and ownership sidecars live. Defaults to beside the session store. |
| `PI_IDENTITY_HEADER`            | The request header naming the caller. Unset means one anonymous user.          |

`PI_RUNTIME_API_KEY_OPENAI_CODEX` keys the `openai-codex` provider: the suffix
lowercases and its underscores become dashes.

`GET /api/pi/health` answers `{ ok, running, threads }`. `running` counts the
sessions mid-turn — a deploy that restarts while it is above zero aborts
someone's answer.

## Artifact desks

Each chat owns one directory, `<PI_ARTIFACTS_DIR>/<threadId>/`, and it is the
only place the agent writes files a user can download. The desk is created
before Pi builds the session, so the system prompt can name it and the agent can
write into it on its first turn.

Two rules make the desk a boundary rather than a convention. A symlink is never
listed and never served — it is the one way out of a desk, and the agent can
make one. And a download resolves the whole path, every intermediate component
included, and the result must still be inside the desk, so `..` and a planted
link are refused by the same check. A dot-named file is hidden from the listing,
which is what gives the agent a `.scratch/` area the user is not offered.

## Feedback and ownership

Both are append-only JSONL under `PI_SIDECAR_DIR`, deliberately outside Pi's
session files: Pi is pre-1.0 and owns its own schema, so a Pi upgrade cannot
lose them.

Feedback is keyed on a **durable Pi entry id**, never a positional one. A
projected assistant message merges a whole run, so several ids can name it; the
verdict is the newest record written against any of them
(`latestPiEntryRecord`), and a message the projection could not name durably
(`hasPiDurableId`) gets no thumbs at all.

Ownership is one line per created chat. Who is asking comes from
[`lib/identity.ts`](lib/identity.ts) — the fork answers "nobody", a deployment
behind an identity-aware proxy names its header with `PI_IDENTITY_HEADER`, and a
header that needs decoding replaces that one function.

## Composer menus

`/` lists every command Pi would accept in this workspace — prompt templates,
skills, and extension-registered commands — and `@` lists workspace files. Both
INSERT text rather than act, so a picked command goes out through the ordinary
send path and can still be given arguments.

**A command cannot be a chat's first message.** `createThread` does not answer
until the message it carries has been admitted, so the chat has no id while Pi
is holding the prompt — and a command that raises a dialog would be waiting on a
client that cannot subscribe to it. Nothing here can tell an interactive command
from a quiet one, so all of them are excluded from that one position: the `/`
menu says so, and Send is blocked with the reason on screen.

cases.new_string:
## The product scenario

`product` is the CP 2c counterpart to `seam`: it checks itself over the app's
own HTTP surface, then hands the browser the part a person has to look at.

Its desks live OUTSIDE the workspace, which is the deployed shape — the world is
read-only and only the desks are writable. `PI_IDENTITY_HEADER=x-harness-user`
stands in for whatever identity-aware proxy a deployment puts in front, so the
ownership stamp is proven without naming IAP anywhere.

The three escapes are the point of the desk section, and they are three
different mistakes: a `..` in the path, a symlink whose TARGET is outside, and a
symlinked DIRECTORY with a perfectly ordinary file behind it. One
resolve-then-contain check refuses all three; a guard that only rejected `..`
would pass the first check and fail the other two.

finding:: the `/` menu made something visible that nothing rendered before —
**Pi discovers user skills from `$HOME/.agents/skills`, keyed on `HOME` and not
on the configured agent dir**, so `PI_CODING_AGENT_DIR` does not isolate them
(0.84.1 `package-manager.js` `userAgentsSkillsDir`). Seam criterion 2 holds for
`~/.pi` and not for this. It is not new behaviour — the per-session prompt has
always been composed from the same discovery — but the menu is the first place a
reader can see it. On a deployment the service user has its own home, so the
practical reach is that user's directory.

### The product leg

Run the scenario, then in the browser:

1. The chat reads right-to-left, the placeholder is «שאל שאלה», the greeting is
   generic Hebrew, and a code block inside an answer stays left-to-right.
2. On a NEW chat, type `/`: the menu says a command cannot start one, Send is
   disabled, and Enter sends nothing.
3. Open the seeded chat: the header shows a cost and a tool count, and under it
   the desk's files as download links.
4. Hover the answer: 👍 and 👎 are there, and the one picked stays lit across a
   reload.
5. Press Stop mid-turn: ONE notice, «צ׳אט נעצר», and the cut message carries
   `data-incomplete="cancelled"`. On `agents/mock-noretry` with
   `MOCK_FAIL_FIRST=1` a genuine failure carries `data-incomplete="error"` and
   keeps its reason above the composer.
6. Below 768px the sidebar is a drawer opened from the header; the pencil
   renames in place; there is no archive and no delete.

+// Every number a play session would make us change lives here, and nowhere else.
+//   METRES  — framing and geometry. The chase camera sits CAM_OFFSET.z = 9.6 m
+//             behind the truck, so a rival further back than ~14 m is off screen
+//             and anything with a positive gap is in frame. Fixed by the camera,
+//             so how fast the player drives cannot change these.
+//   SECONDS — pacing. A dramatic beat lasts the same whether the player is
+//             flooring it or crawling, so these survive any driving style.
+// A rival is never told to "drive". It holds a gap along the course relative to
+// the player, and that gap swings from far behind to briefly ahead and back.
+  tintStrength: 0.72,      // how far each rival's paint pulls toward its color (0..1)
+  gapBehind: 26,           // m — resting gap: a rival waits here, out of sight
+  gapAhead: 18,            // m — top of a surge: this far ahead, in plain view
+  gapDamp: 1.2,            // how fast a rival closes on its target gap
+  headingDamp: 6,          // course tangent is constant per 4 m sample, so damp the step out
+  tiltDamp: 14,            // matches the player truck's surface-conform response
+  surgeSeconds: 15,        // s — one full behind → ahead → behind cycle
+  surgeSharpness: 2.2,     // >1 keeps a rival behind most of the cycle and ahead briefly

## G2 — ownership map and task DAG

**Open as of 2026-08-28.** Both halves of the branch question are answered.
Production work may start on the tasks below, inside the named ownership only.

### File ownership

| Owner | Files |
| --- | --- |
| `session-core` | `rust/model.rs`, `rust/codecs.rs`, session rendering and provider modules, and the visibility, shortening, and tool-filter layer extracted from the branch's `session.rs` |
| `query-semantics` | `rust/search_query.rs` and its generated Unicode tables |
| `search-runtime` | `rust/main.rs`, `rust/lib.rs`, `rust/python_extension.rs`, the lifted inventory, scanner and gate modules, and the search engine and view modules |
| `contract-owner` | `tests/` and all fixtures |
| `reviewer-profiler` | No production files. Gates, harnesses, and review. |

Nobody lifts the branch's `session.rs` wholesale. Agent transcript merging stays

## Deliberate divergences from legacy

**The line.** Preserve legacy behavior, including behavior we think is poor,
whenever legacy produces a usable answer. Diverge only where legacy fails to
produce an answer at all. A hang and a crash cost the user the result.
Verbosity does not.

Every item here goes in `final-change-log.md`.

| Divergence | Reason |
| --- | --- |
| Catastrophic patterns fail loud instead of hanging | Measured: `ch search '(a+)+b'` against 40 consecutive `a` characters does not terminate in CPython within 10 seconds. No timeout, no warning, no interrupt short of killing the process. The guard is a **repair**, not a regression. No golden fixture can own this case, because the oracle produces no answer to record. |
| `COLUMNS="²"` renders instead of crashing | It passes Rich's `isdigit()` and then raises in `int()`. Reproducing a crash on an input where the crash is the bug serves nobody. |
| Warning text keeps its category, drops the source location | A Python warning's `file:line` names a location in the interpreter's source that does not exist in a native binary. Any value is invented. The branch invented one from `CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR`, naming a Python file it deletes — the fabricated-provenance anti-pattern this project already removed once. |
| Colored highlighting is corpus-bounded | Provable parity needs Rich and Pygments, which needs Python, which fails the charter. Stated plainly rather than discovered later. |

per candidate file and exiting 1. It works. Changing it is a product improvement
outside this mission, and smuggling an improvement into a parity rewrite is the
failure this team spent the day guarding against. It goes to the captain as a
separate proposal.

cases.new_string:
## Preserved because they are wrong

The most dangerous class on this mission: a native implementation looks correct,
diverges, and no reviewer objects because the output looks *better*. Full list in
[`preserve-because-wrong.md`](preserve-because-wrong.md), all confirmed by
running the oracle at `8cb4c5f`.

Every fixture pinning these **carries a comment saying the expectation is wrong
on purpose.** Without it the next reader helpfully repairs the fixture and we
ship the divergence through our own contract.

1. **The age label and the age colour disagree by one bucket.** `humanize_age`
   and `age_style` carry separate, unaligned thresholds: `3d` is painted with the
   *week* colour, `2w` gets *month*, `1mo` gets *old*. Driving both from one
   table — the obvious simplification — repaints every coloured result row.
   **Highest risk on the mission**, because `contract-owner`'s comparator
   normalizes the age SGR away, so this is the one dimension where a regression
   fires no gate. Pinned at unit level immediately rather than waiting for the
   clock seam. `humanize_age` also uses 30-day months and 365-day years, so
   360–365 days renders `12mo` before jumping to `1y`.
2. **`collapse_home` matches a string prefix, not a path boundary.**
   `/Users/giladbarneaX/dev/chats` renders `~X/dev/chats`. Reaches the list row
   and the panel title.
3. **`elide_to_width` counts code points**, so wide text overflows its budget:
   `你好你好你好你好` at a budget of 8 comes back unchanged, at 16 columns.
4. **`truncate_middle` counts code points**, so shortening is
   normalization-sensitive: 400 characters survive as NFC, come back as 253 as
   NFD.
5. **Title elision counts code points**, so NFD truncates about nine visible
   characters early against NFC at the same width.

**Scope is wider than titles.** `elide_to_width` has four call sites in
`commands/search.py` across both views plus `formatting.py:152`.
`truncate_middle` reaches `model.py` directly and `shorten_data` at six more
sites, so it surfaces in every `--short` mode. **The codebase already counts in
three different units** — code points here, UTF-16 code units in Pi
`responsePreview` truncation. Any port that unifies them changes behaviour.

22i. **Exhaustive is always exhaustive over a parameterization, and the
    parameterization is the assumption.** The capstone rule; every other
    constraint here is an instance of it.
    *Earned:* `session-core` built a colour oracle on two principles that both
    sounded complete — every colour the product emits, and every value in each
    channel — and it was blind to one of three hazards, because a nearest-match
    argmin is stressed by neither. The float-versus-integer distance disagrees
    with Rich 56 times in 636,056 triples, about one in eleven thousand, and when
    it disagrees it picks an **entirely different** colour rather than an
    adjacent one. Rare enough to survive any sampling, loud enough to be
    unmissable in the wild.

    falsification** — a deliberately wrong implementation, run as part of the
    gate, failing the build if the gate ever stops catching it. Not a check
    performed once. Scope: the colour downgrade, the query engine, the candidate
    gates, and the width and colour-system resolution.

    problem suggests. One chosen from the **failure mode** finds what you would
    otherwise miss.

5. **An oracle event triggers a re-blessing sweep across every artifact carrying
   an oracle stamp**, not only the corpora obviously affected. `rg
   oracle_tree_state` over the desk gives the list — currently nineteen files.
   *Why:* the clock seam was the first oracle event, and it caught the rule's own
   author. Every one of `context-curator`'s eight findings still claimed
   `src/chats clean at 8cb4c5f`. Three are reached through the file that changed.
   All eight re-verified and all eight hold — but the belief that carried them,
   "they live in files nobody touched", was true and still not a proof. **The

mate relayed the general form twice; do not let it into a fixture.

behind, which is what makes them findable.

5. **Title elision counts code points**, so NFD truncates about nine visible

6. **A bool `color=true` resolves colour OFF and metadata colour ON.** Python
   compares `color` against the strings `"always"` and `"auto"`, and a bool
   matches neither — while `metadata_color = color != "never"` is true. There is
   a test named for it.
7. **An empty tool filter list is falsy, so it does not mean "all".**
   `ToolVisibility::Filters(vec![])` reproduces Python's empty-list semantics.
8. **`s=p:128`, `s=8:p` and `s=8:` all raise.** The short-modifier lookahead
   joins the next token and the spec parser then rejects the colon form. The
   lookahead exists to name the whole value **in the error message**, not to
   accept it — which is not what its shape suggests. The valid spelling is

## ⚠ `search-runtime` is down — 2026-08-28

Their session ended without warning while a ruling was in transit. **Nothing was
lost**, which is the entire return on the resume-brief discipline:
`rust/pager.rs`, `terminal.rs`, `clock.rs`, `inventory.rs` and `scanner.rs` are
all in the tree, `cargo check --no-default-features` is green, and
`teammates/search-runtime/` holds a current `RESUME.md`, the promoted handoff,
the 76-case `probes/grammar-oracle.json` and the 12,096-row `color-oracle.tsv`.

**Unowned as a result: the argument grammar (`rust/search.rs`), `rust/main.rs`
routing, and the G4 cutover.** The engine went to `query-semantics` before the
loss. Views were already waiting on `session-core`.

### The ruling they never received — apply it to the grammar

Their last message reported **the seventh branch defect and a sharper finding
underneath it.**

*The seventh defect.* The branch's help text is a static string constant in
`search_help_consts.rs`, asserted against a single fixture. But argparse rewraps
the whole help body at terminal width: **42 lines at 96 columns, 68 at 60**,
differing from the first line. The branch emits identical bytes at every width
and is wrong at all but one. That is the third width defect sharing one blind
spot — every case in the branch's corpus pins `COLUMNS=96`, so a static help
constant, a `COLUMNS`-only helper and a fixed-44 elision all passed 704 of 704
for the same reason. **One unexamined dimension, three defects.**

*The sharper finding.* **The product resolves terminal width two different ways
and they disagree.** argparse goes through `shutil.get_terminal_size`, which is
`int(COLUMNS)` in a try/except and accepts a leading `+`, surrounding whitespace
and fullwidth digits. Rich uses `str.isdigit()` then `int()`. They differ on
`+96`, `0` and `' 96'`. Verified end to end on the real launcher: `--help` at
`COLUMNS=+96` resolves 96 while error wrapping resolves 80, same binary.

**Rulings, recorded here because they never reached their author:**

1. **Two resolvers, and this is not duplication.** `terminal.rs::columns_override`
   stays as Rich's rule for rendered output. The grammar gets its own with
   `shutil` semantics. A single resolver would be the helpful unification this
   team has now caught four times. Name each for what it models.
2. **Split the grammar into two slices.** Slice one is parsing, repairs, mode
   forcing, role normalisation and error bytes — everything except `--help` and
   `-h` — driven straight off the captured 76-case oracle. Slice two is the help
   formatter with its own width-sweep gate at several widths. This keeps the part
   most likely to overrun off the critical path.
3. **No divergence on help output.** It is public surface and legacy produces a
   correct answer at every width, so the line holds: we preserve. Fixtures cannot
   cover a continuous dimension and shelling to Python violates the charter.
4. **Test the narrowing before accepting the 400–600 line estimate.** That figure
   assumed reproducing argparse's general `HelpFormatter`. The parser's content
   is fixed and known — only the wrapping varies with width. If the usage
   assembler does not need the general part-splitting logic, the work may be much
   smaller. Unverified; the first mate has not read that code.

22y. **A claim confirmed only by reading is a lead, not a result.** Source
    reading tells you which inputs a route *reads*. It does not tell you which
    ones change *this* output. An ambient-input enumeration built by reading gave
    seven gaps; measured, three were real and four were inputs Rich genuinely
    consults that do not move the search render.
    **Enforced at the point of use, not by audit:** when an owner builds on a map
    claim, they confirm it by execution or flag it as unconfirmed, and G3 checks
    which stage a claim reached. A sweep would find only the claims already
    marked, and the unmarked ones are the exposure — the same reason the oracle
    grep found only the compliant.
    *Applies to this desk's own maps.* They were written against a tree that has
    moved several times; the engine handoff's blocked table was stale within the
    hour.

### G3 review split — three evidence types, not two

| Reviewer | Evidence type |

**E. Deletion, and only after the byte harness is green.**

**Prerequisite, wider than first ruled: before the oracle is deleted, every
instrument that consults it must have its last consultation stored.** An
instrument not converted by then has silently become a script that cannot run.
I first ruled this as "freeze the fuzz-discovered cases into fixtures" — one
corpus, when it is a property of the whole instrument set.

`reviewer-profiler` audited their eleven: **five die unless converted, two
partly.** Ratio gates become absolute budgets from frozen Python medians; width,
ambient and colour-tier gates freeze Python's bytes as fixtures; the memory
comparison freezes `7.01x + 82` as a constant. `ratio_scaling` **retires** rather
than converting — it exists to prove the ratio gates are properties, and once
they are absolutes the question is moot. An instrument that has answered its
question should be retired, not preserved.

`contract-owner`'s live differential has the same property: it compares `ch
search` against `ch-legacy search`, so the class stops being runnable — **not
broken, over.** Two consequences for whoever runs this slice: do not let it land
while the differential is the only thing that has verified a recent change, and
expect the class's removal to be part of the slice rather than read as a
regression. *That reads as a broken suite six weeks later if nobody wrote down
that it was supposed to expire.*

**The design lesson, from the two instruments that survive by accident.** One
compares a binary against *itself* — closed against full, first byte against
total. One asserts a *stored rule* rather than another route. Neither was
designed for durability; both got it from the shape of the question. **An
instrument that compares against a stored rule, or against itself, is durable by
construction. One that compares against a live peer is not.** Cheaper to re-pose
the question than to freeze the comparison.

behaviour; the byte lock is the proof that survives it.

cases.old_string: ## Runtime sharing
cases.new_string:
## Child session persistence

Every dispatched agent gets a persisted `SessionManager.create(cwd, undefined, { parentSession })` rather than an in-memory one, so its conversation is an ordinary Pi session file from birth. `parentSession` is a *path*, and it records the main session that dispatched the agent — the same field `/fork` uses, surfaced by `SessionManager.list()` as `parentSessionPath`. There is no API to promote an in-memory session to disk later: `SessionManager` fixes `persist` at construction, and both `_persist()` and `_rewriteFile()` return early when it is false, so `setSessionFile()` on an in-memory manager sets a path and writes nothing.

Two ordering constraints follow from `createAgentSession`:

1. **Build the session while its manager is still empty.** Pi writes the `model_change` and `thinking_level_change` entries only on the empty-session path. Seed messages first and those entries never appear, so a resumed child falls back to `findInitialModel` instead of the model it was dispatched with.
2. **Route the inherited snapshot through the session manager.** Persistence runs off message events, so the old `session.agent.state.messages = inherited` assignment never reached the file. `persistInheritedMessages` appends it entry by entry, then the agent state is set to the same list.

That snapshot is already compaction-resolved, so at most one `compactionSummary` leads it. Each role takes its own append method — `appendCompaction`, `branchWithSummary`, `appendCustomMessageEntry`, `appendMessage` — because pi's own compaction and branch bookkeeping locates boundaries by entry type, and a summary written as a plain message entry would be invisible to it. `appendCompaction` wants a `firstKeptEntryId` the replay cannot know, but `buildContextEntries` only consults it for entries *before* the compaction entry; a leading compaction has none, so the value is never read.

The file itself appears on the child's first assistant message (`_persist` defers until then). An agent dispatched with `-i` that never answers therefore leaves nothing behind, while an agent that inherited context has a file immediately.

## Detaching

`d` `d` ends the live child session and drops its widget row. The session file is untouched, and the transcript gets a `pi-user-agents-detached` custom entry naming the session id so it can be resumed later. Both detach paths funnel through `closeRunning` and `removeCompleted`, which is where the announcement is made; joining and session shutdown deliberately do not announce.

## Iteration protocol (added 21:55, per Gilad)

The experiment is not one-shot. Between batches, the main session — the human-judgment lane — runs the epistemic audit: *what do we need to know · what don't we know yet · what did the last batch teach · what do we believe but hold uncertainly · which falsifying questions advance us* → dispatches the next batch accordingly. **Stop rule (saturation):** iterate until results repeat and nothing new is learned for the last couple of iterations — at that point the relevant data-model space is covered, and what has survived is treated as true. The decision bars above are applied to the accumulated evidence, not to iteration 1 alone. All execution is delegated to subagents/teams; the main session keeps only big-picture and judgment.

## Iteration 2 — dispatched 26-07-19 ~23:45 (8 agents, targeted)
